title: Report from Gdansk
paragraphs: -Motivation- I think the fact that scholarships are provided during study abroad under the exchange program with the Medical University of Gdansk deserves more emphasis. It is an excellent system that opens the way to studying abroad even for poor students. I could not have studied abroad without this system. Moreover, what made me think of going to Gdansk in the first place was learning that this system existed.

-A Question- The official language of Poland is Polish. A Japanese medical student who cannot understand Polish cannot do anything as is. I cannot talk with patients, of course, and I cannot read the charts or take part in conferences either. If I were going to do the same things, it is obvious that the amount of information I could obtain would be orders of magnitude greater if I did my clerkship in Japan. So why did I come to Poland? I kept turning over this simple question during my stay. It seems not easy to give a clear and positive answer to this question. Instead, I would like to describe as it is what I experienced and felt in Gdansk.

-Inside the Hospital- I did clerkships in six departments, two weeks each. The first was the emergency department. However, there are not many tertiary-level emergencies to which the emergency department here actually responds, so I mainly did my clerkship in the emergency outpatient clinic. In the emergency outpatient clinic, doctors from the internal medicine, surgery and neurology departments take turns on duty by the day. A different doctor appeared every morning and evening, and each time I asked to do my clerkship. For the local doctors, taking charge of a Japanese student means not only teaching but also interpreting between Polish and English. It is easy to imagine that explaining everything in the examination room in Polish, such as exchanges with patients, the contents of the charts and instructions to nurses, in English that is as unfamiliar to them as it is to Japanese people, while handling a busy workload, takes considerable effort and time. Even the doctors who at first kindly allowed me to do my clerkship were eventually swallowed up by busyness and fatigue, and I came to stand idly in the corridor. Wading into a place where an incomprehensible language flew around in front of me and speaking in English was tiring and I hesitated. I had come all the way to Poland full of enthusiasm, but I hit the language barrier hard with that same momentum and was crushed.

Around that time I met Adam, who was on duty in the outpatient clinic for internal medicine. He always kept me busy. He fired question after question at me. He stood between the patients and me and interpreted simultaneously. He let me help with part of his work. He scolded me, saying I should promote myself more. Moved by his warmth, which went beyond kindness, I began to learn Polish. I stopped blaming anyone other than myself. At such a time, good luck comes along, and I was able to become friends with other doctors who took special notice of the Japanese. I had encounters with patients that seemed to loosen my stiff heart. Polish students volunteered to interpret. Paramedical staff, curious about the Japanese, began to talk to me with gestures. Their poor English and my meager Polish were better than nothing, and thanks to them I was often able to get through boredom. However small it was, I could always find one happy thing a day, and that made me feel happy for the day; I came to have that kind of emotional leeway. Afterward, when my emergency department clerkship period ended and I went to other departments, I still dropped by the emergency outpatient clinic in the evenings.

-Outside the Hospital- Among the many schools of karate, it was probably my greatest piece of luck in Poland that the karate dojo I found in Gdansk was of the Shotokan style, to which I belong. The karate teacher understood English, and not only welcomed me as a Japanese exchange student but even asked me to teach karate to the students. Most of the students were children of high school age or younger, and they became very attached to the foreigner with black eyes and black hair. The adults who were confident in their skills challenged the Japanese in all sorts of ways, and I too was quite desperate not to disgrace the standing of a Japanese black belt. On the way home after practice, walking and chatting noisily with the children, reluctant to part in the time that remained, was a very enjoyable time.

-The Answer- In the end I never came to understand Polish. Because of that, there were many times when I felt frustrated in my clerkships. On the other hand, there were also many times when I benefited from people being interested in me simply because I was Japanese. I realized that the two are, so to speak, two sides of a coin, and that I was only looking at different aspects of one reality. It was three months in which, reflecting the state of my own mind, I swung back and forth between the two. I very much enjoyed teaching karate. I was given a small role in the community, and through it I came into contact with local people, so I felt I was living with both feet planted on the land of Gdansk. The letters that the students read aloud and handed to me on my last day of practice became a treasure I must never forget. My powers of analysis are far too poor to offer a convincing answer to the question of why Poland. However, I think it hints at the shape of the answer that, in the car on my way out of the country, the wish to come back to Gdansk once again welled up naturally. I thank everyone who brought me together with Gdansk, a beautiful city with a long history.
